goal: Decide whether Narra adds named arguments at the call site, such as foo(a = 1, b = 2), amending D12, and in what form

claims.text: D12: a call passes every argument; there is no currying, partial application, pipe, method call, varargs, optional parameters or labeled arguments. Reasons: one call form to read, search and generate; one C function with a fixed parameter list; each function type-checked from its signature.

SPEC section 2: no varargs and no optional parameters; pass an array or a struct with defaults, `File.open(path, OpenOptions { create: true })`. Struct field defaults must be compile-time constants, and a struct literal's type name can be left out when the expected type is known: `{ field: value }`.

Assignment is a statement in Narra (AssignStmt; compound assignment is also statement-only, D76), so `name = expr` is never an expression inside an argument list today. In TypeScript, `foo(a = 1)` assigns 1 to `a` and passes 1.
Parameter counts over all 1477 function declarations in selfhost/src and std (approximate; a parameter of function type may undercount): 0-3 params 1114, 4 params 163, 5-11 params 200.

In selfhost/src and std: 113 lines call with a bare `true`/`false` argument (for example `writeUses(query, places, false)`, `getDirectory(path, true)`), and 97 lines pass a struct literal `Name { ... }` as an argument.

Prior art: Kotlin uses exactly `foo(a = 1)` with named and positional mixing, defaults on parameters, and parameter names part of the source API; Swift makes argument labels part of the function name; Python has keyword arguments and keyword-only parameters; C# uses `foo(a: 1)`; OCaml has labeled arguments `~a:1` tied to currying; Dart has `{}` named parameters. TypeScript/JavaScript have none and use an object parameter with destructuring. Rust has no named arguments after several unaccepted RFCs; Go has none.

evidence.source: Kotlin, Swift, Python, C#, OCaml, Dart language references; rust-lang/rfcs named-arguments threads

claims.text: Every language change is built twice, in the Go compiler and in selfhost/, and keeps the bootstrap fixed point. Calibration: generators L, 482k tokens, 2 review rounds (round 2: three emitter sites kept raw C locals across a yield, and Go and selfhost emitted the same wrong C); block-expressions estimated M, took L, 413k; ternary S took M, 264k; match-block-values S, 137k. M nodes median about 390k.

Roadmap priorities: must = needed for self-hosting; should = spec features real programs need soon; could = spec features with no current user; later = parked. SPEC.md is the source of truth; every feature adds samples and error tests and is built in both compilers.

Narra follows TypeScript syntax where the meaning is the same; where the meaning differs it uses different syntax or a compile error (SPEC.md line 41, D2). Past debates in this repo (local-functions, qualified-enum-constructors, sum-type-syntax) rejected designs where the same text gets a second meaning.
Maintainer direction 2026-11-07: no features that hide which implementation runs (no operator overloading, no implicit calls at operators or scope ends).

evidence.source: maintainer's statement in this session, recorded in user memory

claims.text: Form: an optional name label on a call argument, `foo(flag: true, count: 3)`, using a colon like struct-literal fields and C#/Swift, not `=`. Rules: labels are all-or-nothing after any positional args, must match the parameter names, must appear in declaration order, and every parameter is still passed exactly once. D12 amends from 'no labeled arguments' to 'labels are checked documentation', no defaults, no reordering, so 'a call passes every argument' and the fixed C parameter list stay true.

evidence.detail: `=` is rejected: in TS `foo(a = 1)` is an assignment expression, and Narra has assignment statements only (J3), so the same text would get a second meaning (J9). Colon has no existing meaning at the start of an argument.

claims.ruling_why: conceded in P11: Q1 asks for out-of-order arguments

claims.text: Ship as one S/M node: parser adds an optional name to Arg (Arg already carries the call-site `mutable` marker, so the AST has a per-argument annotation slot), checker compares labels to the callee's parameter names and order, emitter is untouched because labels vanish before codegen. Built in Go then selfhost, with samples and error tests.

evidence.detail: The L-class overruns (generators 482k, block expressions 413k) came from emitter work across yields and temporaries; label-only sugar has none. Arg struct at compiler/internal/narra/ast.go:375.

claims.ruling_why: O1 (unnamed builtin and function-type parameters) and O2 (43 Arg sites, astdump, query, fmt) put it at or above the M median, not 264k

claims.text: Precedent: D27 already makes the call site carry information the declaration holds (`Array.push(mutable xs, v)`), for the same reason of one explicit reading per call. Labels extend that stance to arguments whose meaning is not visible: 113 lines in selfhost/std pass a bare true/false, and 200 functions take 5 or more parameters. Agents reading a call line see the intent without opening the callee.

estimate.unit: bare-bool call lines that gain a label

claims.ruling_why: with O3's correction: about 30 distinct callees, not 113 independent cases

claims.text: Stage 2, separate node after P2 proves out: diagnostics. A wrong or misordered label gets a JSON diagnostic with an exact fix edit (D11 style), and `narrac fmt`/a lint can offer to add labels to bare literal arguments. Stage 2 is droppable without affecting P1/P2.

evidence.source: DECISIONS.md D11 (JSON diagnostics with exact fix edits)
evidence.detail: Exact edits make the migration of existing calls mechanical, so adoption cost is not paid by hand.

claims.ruling_why: fmt is a syntax-only pass (O5); a lint that adds labels is a separate debate

claims.text: Parameter names become public API for labelled calls: renaming a parameter breaks labelled callers. This is the same property Kotlin and Swift accept, and it is contained because unlabelled calls stay valid and the checker reports the rename with the stale label's line.

evidence.source: Kotlin named arguments, Swift argument labels (J6)
evidence.detail: Kotlin keeps positional mixing and treats names as source API; Python keyword args the same. No language reviewed made labels checked-and-optional a source of unsoundness.

claims.text: Cheapest: no language change. Show parameter names as inlay hints from the query CLI/LSP, and keep using a struct argument with defaults for options (SPEC section 2). Costs about zero compiler tokens, preserves D12 untouched. Weakness: hints are not in the source text agents and reviewers read, and a struct needs a declared type per function.
claims.ruling_why: Q1: the maintainer wants the language feature; hints are not in the source text

claims.text: Narrower: labels required only where an argument is a bare literal (`true`, `false`, number, string) for a parameter of bool type, a compile error otherwise. Targets exactly the 113 measured bare-bool lines, with the same parser work as P1 but a smaller rule and no public-API surface for other parameters.
claims.ruling_why: Q1: bool-only required labels do not give out-of-order arguments

claims.text: P2's 'emitter untouched, parser plus checker only' omits the builtin and function-value callees: Go-registered std functions are declared as `Params: []Type{...}` and function types hold `Params []Type`, neither with names, so labels have no names to check against there. Either labels are refused for those callees (a second rule readers must learn) or names are added to every registry in both compilers (Go std_*.go and selfhost builtins.nra).

estimate.unit: Go builtin registrations with unnamed Params in std_*.go (grep count of `Params: []Type`)

claims.ruling_why: the design must say whether labels are refused for builtins and function-type calls or whether names are added to the 22 Go registrations and selfhost builtins

claims.text: Arg is touched in 43 places in the Go compiler, and every AST consumer needs the label: astdump, the query CLI (refs, callers), and the formatter (selfhost fmtexprs.nra, 1340 lines, matched to oxfmt layout). Each is built in both compilers with parity tests, so 'S-to-M, 264k' based on ternary undercounts; the M median is 390k and this touches more consumers than a pure expression.

estimate.unit: tokens (M median) as the likely floor

claims.text: The 113 'bare bool' lines overstate the target: the pattern also matches data pushes such as `Arrays.push(mutable parts, ...true)`, and the trailing-literal calls cluster on about 30 distinct callees (pushScope 7, compositeTypes 5, writeUses/scanEffects/printList/printConditional/emitBlock 4 each). Under P1 labels stay optional, so none of those lines change unless someone edits them.

estimate.unit: distinct callees with a trailing bool literal

evidence.source: grep -rhoE '[A-Za-z_.]+\([^()]*\b(true|false)\)' selfhost/src std | sed -E 's/\(.*//' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

claims.text: Optional, checked-only labels give the weakest form of the feature: no reordering, no defaults, so the only gain is documentation that a caller may skip. A reader cannot rely on labels being present, and a bare `true` stays legal. Meanwhile parameter names become public API (P5), a new rename hazard across the std and selfhost modules with no benefit that a type already provides.

evidence.source: P1 rules; DECISIONS.md D12 (one call form to read, search and generate)
evidence.detail: D12's first reason is one form per call; P1 allows two forms for the same call, which cuts against it.

claims.ruling_why: conceded in O8: Q1 makes reordering the point

claims.text: Fix the bare-bool problem at the declaration, with no language change: replace flag parameters with two-case enums or two named functions (e.g. `writeCallers`/`writeRefs` over `writeUses(.., true)`), so the call reads `Mode.Callers`. Only about 30 callees are involved, which a single refactor PR can cover, and long parameter lists (200 functions with 5 or more) already have the struct-with-defaults route in SPEC section 2.

estimate.unit: callees to refactor, no compiler change

claims.ruling_why: conceded in O9: Q1 wants the language feature; the refactor can still be done on its own

claims.text: P4 (fmt or lint auto-adding labels) needs the formatter to know callee parameter names, so fmt would depend on the checker's resolution (today fmt works on syntax and trivia). That breaks fmt as a syntax-only pass in both compilers; treat as a separate debate, not a droppable stage.

Form: `foo(count = 3, flag = true)`, Kotlin's and the maintainer's spelling. Narra has no assignment expression (J3), so an argument that starts with `Ident =` (not `==`) is unambiguous to parse; the TS reading of `foo(a = 1)` cannot occur, and the checker error for an unknown name says 'no parameter named a'. This answers J9 by there being no second meaning inside Narra; `:` stays the fallback if the maintainer prefers TS-text safety. Mixing: positional arguments first, then named ones; a positional argument after a named one is an error (Kotlin's old rule, one reading per line). Each parameter is passed exactly once, by position or by name, never both. `mutable` composes as `buf = mutable xs`. Reordering is the point, so O4's 'weakest form' objection no longer applies.

evidence.question: Q1
evidence.detail: Named arguments are meant to be out-of-order assignments, like in Kotlin.

claims.ruling_why: `=` is the maintainer's spelling (inbox entry, Q1 'like Kotlin'); O12's TypeScript reading is listed as an inferred choice the maintainer can change to `:` at approval
claims.user_why: Maintainer, 2026-11-07: upheld with the spelling changed to `name: value`, to match struct literal fields and avoid the TypeScript assignment reading (O12).

claims.text: Lowering keeps D12's fixed C parameter list: after name resolution the checker permutes the argument list into declaration order, so the emitter sees an ordinary positional call and gets no change. Evaluation order: Narra does not promise left-to-right evaluation of arguments today (inbox note), and the C call evaluates in an unspecified order, so a reordered call is no worse than a positional one. SPEC states that named-argument calls follow the same rule and that arguments with effects must not depend on order. Hoisting reordered arguments into written-order temporaries is rejected here because it adds emitter work and a promise the language does not make elsewhere.

evidence.source: DECISIONS.md D12 (one C function, fixed parameter list); judge note J1
evidence.detail: Permutation is a checker rewrite of Args before codegen. The AST keeps the written labels and order for astdump, query and fmt, so a rewritten copy for emit is needed, not an in-place edit.

claims.ruling_why: the permutation in the checker stands, but leaving evaluation order unspecified does not: O6 (written-order evaluation, as in Kotlin, and the open PR #96 defect)

claims.text: Callees without parameter names: a labelled call is allowed only when the callee resolves to a declaration with parameter names (user functions, imports, std functions declared in .nra). Calls through function values and unnamed Go-registered builtins (22 `Params: []Type` registrations) get one error, 'this callee has no parameter names, pass arguments by position', so no registry changes are needed in stage 1. Names are added to builtins only when someone needs them. One rule, stated in the error text and the SPEC.

Defaults are a separate later decision, not part of this node. Stage 1 requires every parameter to be passed (by name or position), so D12's 'a call passes every argument' survives and only the 'no labeled arguments' clause of D12 is amended. If defaults follow, they reuse the struct-field rule of SPEC section 2 (compile-time constants) and would amend D12 again with their own debate. The maintainer's Q1 answer did not mention defaults.

Size and order, against O2: three nodes, each built in Go then selfhost. N1 syntax: Arg gets a name, parser, astdump, fmt, in both compilers. N2 checker: resolve names, reject duplicates and missing and bad mixing, permute for emit. N3 query CLI (refs, callers) reads labelled calls. Estimate about 500k tokens in total, above the M median 390k as O2 says, with N1 about 150k, N2 about 250k, N3 about 100k. N1 can merge alone; N2 is the one that carries the generator-style risk of two compilers emitting the same wrong thing, so it needs a differential sample test in both.

evidence.detail: Priced as an M that grew to L, matching block expressions (413k) plus consumer parity work.

P7's 'no emitter change, order unspecified' leans on an open defect: the inbox (PR #96 review) lists non-left-to-right argument evaluation as a bug to fix in both emitters or reject by a check. Once that is fixed, a permuted call must evaluate in written order, so reordered arguments need temporaries in the emitter; Kotlin, the maintainer's reference, evaluates in written order. The emitter already hoists in index order for self tail calls (emit_call.go tailJump), which would also need written order.

Two views of one call is a bug source and is not priced in N2's 250k; with O6 the total is nearer 650k than 500k.

P8 makes label eligibility depend on how the callee was declared. The most-called functions are Go builtins with no names (Arrays.length 711, Arrays.push 651, Arrays.values 610 calls in selfhost/src) and are position-only, while source functions accept labels. Neither the call site nor the signature tells an agent which kind it has; the user learns by error. The loss is small because those callees take 1 to 2 arguments.

claims.text: Without defaults, Kotlin-style reordering lets a caller name only what it wants to read, but every parameter must still be passed, so a call gains no brevity and the 200 functions with 5 or more parameters stay as long. The maintainer's Kotlin reference usually comes with defaults; shipping reordering first may produce a second amend of D12 within weeks. The choice changes the structure, so ask.

evidence.source: evidence/params.txt (J4): 200 functions with 5-11 parameters; Kotlin named arguments docs (J6)

claims.text: P6 claims `Ident =` is unambiguous because Narra has no assignment expression, but J9's past debates (local-functions, qualified-enum-constructors) rejected the same text with a second meaning, and the TS-trained agents that write most Narra read `f(a = 1)` as an assignment. A mistaken `f(x = y)` meaning `x == y` becomes a named argument when f has a parameter x, and the checker reports it only if the types differ.

evidence.detail: Low because the maintainer chose the spelling; the colon remains the fallback P6 names.

questions.ask: What should named arguments give you? (a) Readable calls only: optional `foo(flag: true)` labels checked against parameter names, same order, every argument still passed (about 390k tokens). (b) Kotlin-style: labels plus parameter defaults and any order, which reverses D12's 'a call passes every argument' and needs a larger design. (c) No language change: refactor the ~30 flag-taking functions to enums or separate functions, and keep option structs.
questions.answer: Named arguments are meant to be out-of-order assignments, like in Kotlin (maintainer, 2026-11-07). Parameter defaults were not mentioned.

questions.ask: Should named arguments also bring parameter defaults, so a call may omit a parameter, as in Kotlin? Without defaults, a call still passes every argument and only reordering and labels are gained; with defaults, D12's 'a call passes every argument' is reversed and the design grows.
questions.answer: Defaults later: ship named, reorderable arguments first and decide parameter defaults in a separate debate (maintainer, 2026-11-07).
